title: Cap-and-Spill: Two-Pass CUDA-Graph MoE Dispatch Without Worst-Case Padding

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to reduce padding waste in CUDA-graph-captured MoE AllToAll dispatch while keeping fixed buffer sizes. None of the prior papers explicitly address this specific objective. Papers like [6] and [9] discuss MoE inference optimizations, but their focus is on load balancing, sparsity-aware caching, or sharding, not on reducing padding waste in CUDA-graph-captured dispatch. Similarly, papers like [19] and [4] discuss CUDA graph optimizations, but they do not address padding waste or fixed buffer sizes in MoE dispatch.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, Cap-and-Spill, involves a two-pass CUDA-graph-compatible dispatch algorithm using quantile-based buffer capacity (C = Q99) for the first pass and a second pass for overflow tokens. None of the prior papers propose a substantively equivalent mechanism. Papers like [6], [9], and [11] discuss MoE routing mechanisms, but they do not involve quantile-based buffer capacity or a two-pass dispatch algorithm. Papers like [19] and [4] discuss CUDA graph optimizations, but they focus on scheduling or kernel launch overhead, not on buffer capacity or overflow handling.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves maintaining fixed buffers for both passes to ensure CUDA-graph compatibility and demonstrating that unconditional two-pass execution outperforms conditional execution by eliminating synchronization overhead. Papers like [19] and [4] discuss CUDA graph evaluation setups, but they do not use the same evaluation design. No prior paper evaluates a two-pass dispatch algorithm with fixed buffers for CUDA-graph compatibility or compares unconditional versus conditional execution in this context. Thus, the evaluation design appears to be novel.

### Domain
The domain is distributed MoE inference systems. Papers like [6], [9], [11], and [20] work in the same general application area of MoE inference systems, even though they target different specific sub-problems (e.g., load balancing, sparsity-aware caching, dynamic routing). Therefore, the domain is covered.
